newsitem.title: INDIA: India aviation policy reversal dismays investors.
newsitem.headline: India aviation policy reversal dismays investors.

text.p: A recent flip-flop in Indian aviation policy barring foreign airlines from taking stakes in the domestic sector sends worrisome signals about the pace of economic reform, analysts and businessmen said on Sunday.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's crisis-ridden cabinet on Tuesday prohibited foreign airlines from taking stakes in domestic ventures, though it let other foreign investors in.

"This decision will send out negative signals, just as the government was doing fine on other economic fronts," said V. Raghuraman, secretary-general of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham).
A direct casualty of the new rule is a proposed tie-up between India's largest business group, the Tatas, and Singapore Airlines, to set up a $600 million domestic network.

"It's a case of India shooting itself in the foot. Very few airlines can stand alone nowadays. A monopoly situation causes all sorts of inefficiencies," said Graham Hayward, executive director of the Singapore International Chamber of Commerce.
The Tatas planned to take a 60 percent stake in the airline, and SIA the rest, according to a February 1995 proposal, which the government sat on for two years.

It became the focus of a high-profile battle by Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim to protect state-run airlines Air-India, which operates on international routes, and Indian Airlines, which flies domestic routes.

"I think it's very sectoral. They don't want to liberalise the airline sector for whatever reason, but that doesn't mean that in other sectors they won't do that," said Dilip Ratha, senior economist at W.I. Carr stockbrokerage in Singapore.
He said it would not make foreign investors more cautious about India because they were already very cautious.

India hopes to attract $10 billion in foreign direct investment annually over the next few years, mainly to improve its overburdened infrastructure to support economic growth of around seven percent a year.

Foreign direct investment approvals totalled $26.7 billion between August 1991 and December 1996. And in the nine months April to December 1996 the figure was only marginally up on the $1.5 billion for the same period a year earlier.
A strategist with a foreign investment bank said there were still grounds for hope that the civil aviation ministry will drop its objections to foreign airlines entering India's market.
"If one looks at it coolly it is probably just a short-term phenomenon, the result of animosity between the industry minister and the civil aviation minister," he said.

Indian Airlines is closer to moving into the black. On Friday it reported a 1996/97 net loss of 407.5 million rupees against a loss of 1.09 billion 1995/96. It forecast net profit in 1997/98 at 953 million rupees.
The cabinet also limited foreign firms that are not airlines to 40 percent equity stakes in domestic airlines.
The moves have radically affected Jet Airways, India's largest private airline, in which two foreign airlines have stakes.
Gulf Air Holdings and Kuwait Airways each have 20 percent stakes valued at $4 million in Jet Airways, whose fleet of 12 aircraft operates 74 flights each day to 23 destinations.

Jet Airways would divest its foreign equity, an airline official told Reuters. "The policy decision has been taken. We will also disinvest and go by the government requirements," he said. The government has fixed a six-month deadline for divestment.
No other country allowed international carriers to operate its domestic services, said an aviation analyst who did not want to be named. "Why should India be any different?" he asked.
India began opening its aviation sector to private enterprise under an economic liberalisation programme launched by then prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in 1991.

A dozen domestic airlines quickly sprang up, but were winnowed down to a handful by crippling fuel and maintenance costs, low occupancy rates, and government laws that force them to fly to remote, unprofitable regions.
Last year the Civil Aviation Ministry began reviewing policies governing foreign equity stakes in domestic airlines.
India's creaking infrastructure has also slowed growth in air traffic.
